items.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
items.title_original: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

items.title: 研究人员开发 AI 系统：可通过 Wi‑Fi 信号识别隐藏手枪
items.title_original: 研究人员开发 AI 系统：可通过 Wi‑Fi 信号识别隐藏手枪
items.summary: IT之家 10 月 19 日消息，瑞典国防研究局（FOI）的一组 AI 研究人员开发出一套 AI 系统，能够利用 Wi‑Fi 信号识别隐藏的手枪，可以作为可见光摄像头、笨重金属探测器之外的非侵入式替代方案。相关论文于 10 月 13 日发布在 arXiv 平台，这套名为 WiFireNet 的系统，通过分析物体对环境 Wi‑Fi 信号造成扰动所产生的信道状态信息（CSI）完成识别。整套系统由 Wi‑Fi 发射端、接收端以及 WiFireNet 人工智能模型构成。 普通 Wi‑Fi 信号在传播途中遇到物体时，会根据物体的形状、摆放角度与材质，发生穿透和反射，产生独有的信号特征。这类数据就是信道状态信息，对其分析可以实现较高精度的物体识别。安全领域研究人员此前已经公开过一项技术：普通 Wi‑Fi 路由器识别人体的准确率可达 99.5%。 为搭建 WiFireNet 系统，研究人员首先构建了名为 WiFire Dataset 的数据集。他们同步录制 RGB 视频，同时采集携带各类物品（从手机到手枪）行走的人所反射的 Wi‑Fi 信号。研究人员在这份海量数据集上训练深度学习模型，借助视频片段，把隐藏手枪的视觉特征和它对应的 Wi‑Fi 特征（信道状态信息）建立映射。为保证系统能够把手枪和外形、材质相近的日常物品区分开，训练素材包含塑料手枪、金属水杯、真金属手枪以及手机的采集记录。 训练完成后，WiFireNet 仅依靠 Wi‑Fi 信道状态信息就可以检测隐藏手枪，但精度存在波动。在受控实验环境中，狭小室内空间最多同时追踪四名移动人员，这套系统检测手枪的平均精确率为 72.5%。但如果提出更严格的定位要求，例如精准定位武器在携带者身上的具体位置，精确率会下降至 53.8%。当遇到陌生、未经过测试的室内布局时，神经网络识别效果也会明显变差。 该系统目前仍处于实验阶段，研究团队规划了后续优化路线。原型机采用经过改造的老旧 1999 年 IEEE 802.11a 无线标准来验证原理。下一阶段将采用 Wi‑Fi 7、Wi‑Fi 8 现代无线网络，获取分辨率更高的信道状态信息，提升检测性能。研究团队将项目开源，放出代码、模型和数据集，推动该领域后续研究。 IT之家注意到，基于 Wi‑Fi 感知的监控技术正受到越来越多关注，其无需复杂设备与部署。但批评者认为，这项技术可以广泛部署，同时缺少对应的监管框架，会带来严重的隐私隐患。

items.title: SIM-UT: A User Simulation based Evaluation Framework for Medical Triage Chatbots
items.title_original: SIM-UT: A User Simulation based Evaluation Framework for Medical Triage Chatbots
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based chat agents are increasingly used for complex, multi-turn, multilingual medical triage in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet evaluation methods focus on single-turn, English-only benchmarks that primarily test the chatbots' knowledge. In practice, users are often confused, overwhelmed, or emotionally vulnerable, giving unclear, misspelled single-word answers or long messages in regional dialects, and the context of a conversation can shift rapidly. We propose SIM-UT (Simulation of User Behaviour for Triage), a multi-turn, simulation-based evaluation method that identifies ecologically valid, contextually relevant failure modes of LLM-based triage chat agents. Using SIM-UT, we evaluated three real-world WhatsApp-based health chatbots: a respiratory screening programme in India, a hearing health support programme in South Africa, and a diabetes and lifestyle coaching agent in Kenya. We compared a medically fine-tuned open model (MedGemma) against general-purpose frontier models (ChatGPT and Claude) across 5,000+ multilingual simulated conversation turns grounded in the personas, constraints, and communication patterns of the real user populations, over 2-4 iterative rounds. A key failure mode emerged in both model families: de-escalation risk. The agents initially identified medical emergencies correctly, but when the user minimised the symptoms without introducing new clinical information, they de-escalated, exhibiting clinically dangerous sycophancy, for example agreeing that vaginal bleeding in pregnancy was "not a problem" or that decreased fetal movements at 32 weeks "can be normal". We recommend user simulation-based behavioural evaluation, grounded in real user context and covering adversarial and edge cases, as standard practice for triage chatbots in production, so that safeguards can be added before deployment or in subsequent iterations.

items.title: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
items.title_original: Omni-Woodpecker: Hallucination Correction via Evidence-Prior Rebalancing for Omni LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent Omni LLMs (OLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in joint audio-visual reasoning, yet cross-modal hallucinations remain a major challenge. Existing mitigation methods mainly operate at the output level, overlooking the entanglement of grounding evidence and learned priors within fused representations. To address this issue, we propose Omni-Woodpecker (OWP), a training-free framework that shifts hallucination mitigation from output-level manipulation to conflict-conditioned representation rebalancing. Specifically, OWP first identifies cross-modal conflicts from complementary modality-specific views. It then employs orthogonal decomposition to separate grounding evidence from competing priors within the hidden states. Finally, OWP adaptively rebalances fused representations by suppressing misleading priors and restoring ignored evidence before decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and strong cross-architecture generalization of OWP. Using Qwen2.5-Omni-7B as the backbone, OWP improves performance by 12.9 and 8.6 points on CMM and AVHBench, respectively, while consistently achieving gains of 0.67-2.25 points across four general OLLM reasoning benchmarks. Furthermore, OWP generalizes effectively to VideoLLaMA2-AV, improving performance by 4.6 and 3.9 points on the same benchmarks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ZiiJianLiu/Omni-Woodpecker

items.title: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
items.title_original: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. To address this, we present MedPAO-Assist, an edge-deployable agentic framework that generates structured radiology reports directly from radiologist dictation and voice commands, requiring only $\approx3.3$ GB peak RAM and achieving an average end-to-end latency of $\approx31$ seconds on a standard laptop CPU through an asynchronous, multi-threaded execution pipeline. The system currently supports four major imaging modalities -- Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI. To our knowledge, it is among the earliest agentic systems to run its entire pipeline with a Small Language Model (SLM) in the 0.6B-parameter range. This multi-agent architecture, built around an Extract-Ground-Generate paradigm, performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase, together forming a fully "no-touch" reporting workflow that requires no keyboard input, external API calls, or internet connectivity. We evaluate each pipeline stage individually -- concept extraction, ontology grounding, and concept categorization and report hardware profiling results demonstrating the system's feasibility for real-time, CPU-only clinical deployment.

items.title: Hunyuan-A13B Technical Report
items.title_original: Hunyuan-A13B Technical Report
items.summary: arXiv:2609.27284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Hunyuan-A13B, an open-source large language model based on a Mixture-of-Experts architecture. It contains 80 billion total parameters but activates only 13 billion during inference, balancing model capability, computational efficiency, and deployment cost. The model is pretrained on a rigorously filtered 20T-token corpus with enhanced STEM data curation, improving factual reliability and reasoning ability. High-quality supervised fine-tuning and large-scale reinforcement learning further enhance its overall performance. Hunyuan-A13B also introduces a dual-mode Chain-of-Thought framework that adapts reasoning depth to task complexity: fast thinking for routine queries and slow thinking for complex, multi-step problems. Evaluations show competitive performance across mathematics, science, programming, general language understanding, and agent tasks, often approaching that of much larger models. Its high inference throughput makes it suitable for latency-sensitive applications. We release Hunyuan-A13B to support open research and practical LLM deployment.

items.title: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
items.title_original: Stealth Apart, Harm Together: Skill Cascading Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2609.30383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A skill is a modular package of natural-language instructions, executable scripts, and reference resources that an agent can load at runtime to extend its capabilities for a specific task. Skill-based agent systems therefore enable flexible reuse of third-party capabilities, but the openness of this skill ecosystem also opens up a new attack surface. Prior work has focused on vulnerabilities within individual skills, but little attention has been paid to risks that arise from interactions across skills. In this paper, we introduce skill cascading attacks, a threat paradigm in which a malicious objective is distributed across multiple skills so that each modification looks benign in isolation, yet their combined execution is harmful. For instance, in a prescription-review pipeline, the first skill weakens signals of recently discontinued medications in the extracted history, the second downgrades the severity of any drug interaction tied to them, and the third suppresses the resulting low-priority alert in the final summary, so that a severe drug-interaction warning silently disappears before reaching the physician. To systematically study this safety blind spot, we develop SkillCascade, an automated multi-agent red-teaming framework, and release SkillCascade-Bench, a benchmark of 213 validated cascading test cases across multiple agent systems and domains. Across representative agents (e.g., OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and LLM backbones, cascaded interactions reliably induce harmful behaviors while evading existing per-skill scanners and runtime monitors. Our findings highlight a gap between component-level integrity and system-level safety, and call for defenses that reason over cross-skill interactions rather than individual skills in isolation.

items.title: 要帮车企跟上中国同行进度，日本创企 EpicAI 拟用 AI 加速车辆设计评审
items.title_original: 要帮车企跟上中国同行进度，日本创企 EpicAI 拟用 AI 加速车辆设计评审
items.summary: IT之家 10 月 23 日消息，据《日经亚洲》22 日报道，日本 AI 初创公司 EpicAI 计划 帮助日本车企利用 AI 加快新车设计评审 ，以应对中国车企 不断缩短新车开发周期 带来的竞争压力。 面对日益激烈的市场竞争，一向谨慎的日本车企开始改变观念，寻找降低研发成本的方法。EpicAI 希望借此推广旗下软件，大幅减少新车设计所需的时间和人力。 EpicAI 脱胎于东京科学大学，计划从 2027 年春季起向多家日本车企引入软件。公司称，此前的试用获得了客户的积极评价。 EpicAI CEO 横山敬一谈到了日本车企大幅压缩研发周期的计划。“比如，要把设计流程的时间缩短一半，绝非易事。要解决这些难题，就必须 采用 AI 这样的突破性技术工具 。” EpicAI 成立于 2023 年，总部设在东京，拥有约 50 名员工，主要提供 AI 咨询和定制 AI 解决方案，客户包括汽车零部件制造商电装、特斯拉供应商松下等日本大型企业。 横山敬一曾在日本知名 AI 研究人员松尾丰的研究室工作。松尾丰长期参与日本 AI 政策制定，并担任日本政府 AI 战略专家小组主席。 EpicAI 希望利用 AI 自动完成部分车辆设计评审工作， 帮助车企提前发现潜在故障 。报道提到，严格的设计审查长期以来是日本汽车安全性和可靠性的重要保障，但繁琐的流程也越来越不利于加快新车研发。 EpicAI 重点改进的是汽车行业广泛采用的“失效模式与影响分析”，即由工程师检查零部件或系统可能出现的故障，并评估这些故障会造成什么后果。横山敬一指出，许多汽车召回并不是因为生产质量出了问题，而是 设计时未能预见某些故障风险 ，因此这项分析是汽车质量控制的重要环节。 据横山敬一介绍，工程师仅对一个零部件进行设计评审，就可能需要 花费约 200 个小时 ，成为新车研发中相当耗时的环节。 IT之家从报道中获悉，EpicAI 希望利用旗下软件，将这项工作所需的时间从约 200 个小时 缩短至几小时 。 软件采用多个生成式 AI 模型协同工作，分别分析零部件技术规格、识别潜在风险、评估故障发生的可能情形，并相互核对分析结果，以减少错误。 横山敬一称，软件将首先在 多家日本车企的部分部门 投入使用，是否扩大应用范围还需要进一步商讨。 伊藤忠总研执行研究员深尾三四郎指出，中国车企通过接连推出新车型不断积累经验，产品也因此越来越有吸引力。“要与中国竞争对手抗衡，日本车企比以往任何时候都更需要加强品牌建设。AI 是实现目标的手段，而不是目的本身。”

items.title: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback
items.title_original: Steerable Pluralistic Policy Alignment from Anonymized Crowd Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.

items.title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
items.title_original: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.

items.title: GAV: A scientific experimentation environment for PDE agents
items.title_original: GAV: A scientific experimentation environment for PDE agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable feedback is essential for coding agents to develop programs for partial differential equations (PDEs). Yet evaluating these programs on new PDE problems often requires expensive reference computations, while fixed datasets restrict the range of experiments. We introduce Generator-Agent-Verifier (GAV), a scientific experimentation environment that makes new PDE problems verifiable by construction. The Generator learns a distribution of continuous reference solutions using data from numerical simulations or experimental measurements to represent a target physical regime. Using the method of manufactured solutions, it works backward from the generated reference solutions to construct matching PDE problems without a separate numerical solve. The Agent designs experiments, investigates failures, and iteratively improves its program. The Verifier evaluates candidate programs against the reference solutions and provides numerical feedback on accuracy and computational cost. This feedback can also guide the generation of new problems that probe the current program's weaknesses. We provide a theoretical analysis of evaluation reliability and guided development. Experiments on Navier-Stokes and Vlasov-Poisson-type equations across different data sources and regimes demonstrate the effectiveness of GAV. In particular, on the numerical Navier-Stokes task, GAV reduces the mean test error of three existing PDE agents by more than an order of magnitude relative to their original setups. Code is available at https://github.com/PotatoJnny/PDE-GAV.

items.title: 中国科学家首次用中国大模型攻克世界级数学难题，曾困扰学界 30 余年
items.title_original: 中国科学家首次用中国大模型攻克世界级数学难题，曾困扰学界 30 余年
items.summary: IT之家 10 月 15 日消息，上海人工智能实验室今日发文，困扰数学界 30 余年的世界级难题 —— 三维 Ghys 猜想 迎来了破解。 上海人工智能实验室访问学者、大湾区大学教授许地生团队依托书生科学多模态大模型 S2（书生-S2），基于“通专融合”技术路径， 通过人机协同完成了三维 Ghys 猜想证明 。 北京大学董彬教授、刘若川院士团队利用其开发的 SHEAF 框架对本次证明完成形式化验证，验证了这一工作的正确性。 这标志着中国科学家首次用中国大模型攻克世界级数学难题 。 Ghys 猜想由法国数学家艾蒂安 · 吉斯（Étienne Ghys）于 1995 年提出，猜测每一个紧致复流形上的全纯 Anosov 系统，都双全纯共轭于某个复 infra-幂零流形上的全纯仿射自同构。该问题兼具理论难度与学科标志性价值，被动力系统领域数学专家公认为该领域重要的长期公开问题之一，是检验数学推理能力的一块试金石。 相关论文已在预印本平台（arXiv）发布，其形式化代码也在 Github 平台公开。IT之家附链接如下： https://github.com/frenzymath/HolomorphicAnosov 上海人工智能实验室表示，本项研究的意义还在于验证了一种新的科研范式。传统数学研究依赖个体天才的漫长摸索，而本次攻关将专家直觉系统性接入机器求解回路，形成“系统探索 — 专家判断 — 成果积累 — 反馈修正”的闭环。 这一范式可复制推广至更多“搜索空间巨大而专家稀缺”的基础研究领域，实现更多“从 0 到 1”的原始创新突破 。 接下来，依托本次研究跑通的完整能力闭环，团队将进一步封装为书生 · 端砚科学发现平台可复用的数学验证模块，供后续科学问题研究直接调用。同时，以三维 Ghys 猜想的突破作为起点， 上海人工智能实验室将沉淀的推理能力扩展应用于数学结构同源的其他学科 ；取得新突破后，再将新推理能力封装回端砚平台复用，与更多学科结合寻求下一轮突破，形成“突破 — 封装 — 复用 — 再突破”的自进化飞轮。

items.title: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark
items.title_original: Synthetic-to-Real Code-Switched ASR: A Spontaneous Nepali-English Podcast Benchmark
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nepali-English code-switched conversational speech presents severe challenges for automatic speech recognition (ASR), chiefly through script confusion (inappropriate mixing of Devanagari and Latin orthography) and elevated error rates at language switch points. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can adapt multilingual foundation models, but human code-switched audio is expensive to collect and annotate. We curate a new benchmark of 13,044 spontaneous podcast utterances (15.45 h total; 10,214 test, 2,830 dev), audited and verified to eliminate machine translation leakages and acoustic loops. We investigate a two-stage synthetic-to-real adaptation framework: Stage 1 applies SFT on 0.95 h of speech synthesized via a multi-speaker, dual-engine TTS pipeline; Stage 2 explores Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with transcription and script rewards. We find that synthetic SFT provides the primary cross-domain transfer to spontaneous human speech, reducing Mixed Error Rate (MER) from 23.40% to 21.52% (-1.88 pp) and switch-point error rate (SPER) from 35.89% to 28.77% (-7.12 pp). Subsequent GRPO yields small, statistically significant adjustments on 173 test utterances (1.69%), driving English script confusion (SCR_en) from 6.45% to 6.36% (p <= 0.001) and SPER to 28.70% (p = 0.022 clustered). Crucially, ablation reveals that in this SFT-converged encoder-decoder setting, an auxiliary script reward term yields performance identical to MER-only optimization because rollout candidate groups exhibit near-zero script variance on synthetic data. On monolingual benchmarks, SFT improves Nepali MER by 2.71 pp (stabilizing at 18.42% after GRPO, a 2.38 pp gain over baseline) while preserving English lexical WER (3.38% vs. 3.33%). Verified transcripts, timestamps, episode metadata, and reconstruction scripts are publicly released.

items.title: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
items.title_original: Theoretical and Practical Advances in Hierarchical Bayesian Deep Learning Methodology
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.

items.title: Temporal transformer CAN encoder with federated lightweight heads for anomaly detection
items.title_original: Temporal transformer CAN encoder with federated lightweight heads for anomaly detection
items.summary: arXiv:2610.10613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern vehicles rely on large numbers of Electronic Control Units (ECUs) that constantly exchange information over the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus. Due to the rapidity, structure, and repetition of this communication, even slight variations in timing, payload values, or message patterns can point to unusual activity. Whether due to errors, malfunctions, or deliberate interference, these anomalies are frequently subtle and challenging to identify with conventional methods that handle messages separately or rely on manually created rules. Motivated by this gap, we present a privacy-preserving framework for anomaly detection in in-vehicle networks, based on a Temporal Transformer CAN Encoder with Federated Lightweight Heads, to better capture these irregularities. The detection of subtle temporal and contextual anomalies is made possible by a lightweight Transformer encoder that learns how these signals evolve over time, while a federated learning mechanism enables several vehicles or ECUs to work together to improve a shared model without exchanging raw CAN data. This combination of federated learning and temporal sequence modeling provides robust anomaly detection performance while maintaining efficiency and privacy, according to experiments conducted on open-source datasets.

items.title: Leveraging LLM-Generated Explanations for Detecting Emotionally Rewritten Fake News
items.title_original: Leveraging LLM-Generated Explanations for Detecting Emotionally Rewritten Fake News
items.summary: arXiv:2610.08835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spread of fake news may cause severe social consequences. Existing fake news detection methods mainly focus on stylistic variations or incorporate external information such as explanations. However, news articles are often rewritten under different emotional backgrounds while preserving their underlying factual claims, which may affect the robustness of detection models. In this work, we investigate fake news detec- tion under fact-preserving emotional variations. To study this problem, we construct emotion-rewritten test sets and generate explanations from the original news articles as stable background knowledge. We then propose a Gated Cross Attention (GCA) framework that adaptively integrates emotionally rewritten news with the corresponding explanations, enabling the model to focus on informative explanation content while reducing potential mismatches caused by emotional reframing. Experiments on PolitiFact, GossipCop, and LUN demonstrate that the proposed method achieves notable improvements under multiple emotional conditions on PolitiFact and LUN, while maintaining competitive performance on GossipCop. We further analyze the effects of explanation guidance and gating mechanisms under different emotional conditions. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/Flulike/fakenews gca .

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars , here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles . _all_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
_all_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
_all_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. Via Hacker News Tags: git , migrations , version-control , ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , agentic-engineering

_all_articles.title: LaTeX renderer
_all_articles.title_original: LaTeX renderer
_all_articles.summary: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . Tags: latex , paul-ford , tools , urls , ai , generative-ai , llms

_all_articles.title: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust
_all_articles.title_original: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust
_all_articles.summary: Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do? Tags: rdf , semantic-web , sqlite , ai , rust , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code

_all_articles.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
_all_articles.title_original: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
_all_articles.summary: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

_all_articles.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
_all_articles.title_original: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
_all_articles.summary: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A "Daily Op" challenge Ranks and achievements ( Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here's a shared transcript . I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here - it looked like this: It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here - it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Openers : pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts. Call-down powers : Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike. Objectives and salvage : Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap. Feel : combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer. Command : battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement. New modes : Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign. Progression : heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. v5: Battle Drones goes 3D After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 ( play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 ( play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft. v8: Archipelago I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases. I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this: v10: Goliath, and agent battles I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim , or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be. Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it [...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech The end result is really cool . Your browser does not support HTML video. Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map. Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area. Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map! The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built. There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths: Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units. Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one). Agent battles The other v10 feature is agent battles . In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game? Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...] Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles - here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna , and here's that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses. The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here . There are a few more replays like this linked in the README . I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future. v11: Random Maps This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target: Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative. Here's the transcript , and an image Claude generated to show me its work: v12: Multiplayer via sound I only just got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other! This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept: Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals Build a version of that for battledrones Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well! Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game. Some thoughts I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results. Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug. This morning ( via Hacker News ) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop . I wouldn't personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this - it's still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project. ... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build! A few other observations from this project: Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out. This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached. Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts. Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects. For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay. Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition. I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked. Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe , the Model browser , the Agent vs. Agent debug tool , and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven't even explored myself. Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame). Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt. I'm still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from. Update: Online multiplayer support Earlier in this article I said: Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug. Then I tried playing the multiplayer version with Natalie... and the high pitched modem sounds gave her a nasty headache! That's a pretty bad bug. I added a warning and was then inspired to build proper network multiplayer. I tried getting WebRTC to work but couldn't get a connection going between two of my own devices even on my own WiFi network, so I had Claude build a simple, stateless WebSockets relay server instead: If I wanted to support multiplayer between two devices at a very low cost without storing any state on the server could I do that with a tiny asyncio web server running on the cheapest Fly instance? Build the server and the fly.toml for deploying it, use Fly application name battledrones-relay - put that in a folder in the repo, include deploy instructions in the README in that folder Here's the resulting server . Since this scales to zero and runs on a single Fly.io shared-cpu-1x instance it should cost me no more than $2.19/month - and that's if it stays hot and serving connections the whole time. Battle Drones now supports online multiplayer. Click "Duel a friend online", then either share the resulting room URL via your messaging app of choice or have them snap a picture of the displayed QR Code. I also added a feature where you can copy JSON of the match once it has ended and then feed that into the replay feature to rewatch your game. I didn't expect to introduce online multiplayer this soon, but the headache bug felt like it warranted an urgent alternative. _all_articles.summary: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation News today from Anthropic: We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). I'm pleased to note I called this one last December , when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard": I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF , recently the new home of the MCP specification. Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to " Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body ". _all_articles.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
_all_articles.title_original: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
_all_articles.summary: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. What we built We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that Four working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSS Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages Integration with my site search engine It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Finishing it with a review Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. The end result You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.
